hook_text: In 1842 a government report gave the average age at death for labourers in Manchester. It was seventeen.
clip_script: Seventeen. That was the average age at death for labourers' families in Manchester in 1842, according to Edwin Chadwick's report. For wealthy families it was thirty-eight. Why? Walk into a working-class court. Back-to-back houses, windows on one side only. A family of seven in two rooms, plus lodgers. The poorest live in cellars that flood when it rains. One toilet, a hole over a pit, for twenty families. One tap, fed from the river where the sewage goes. Cholera, typhoid, typhus and tuberculosis do the rest, and so many babies die that the average age crashes. Then a doctor named John Snow marks every cholera death in Soho on a map, and they cluster around one water pump. Dirty water was the killer. Sewers and clean water followed, slowly. And if you fell into poverty? The workhouse, designed to be worse than the worst job outside.
visual_style: A large number 17 on a whiteboard, then a cutaway of a back-to-back court with a single privy and pump; dots appearing on a street map around one pump; finally a heavy workhouse door closing.
pacing: A stark number, a slow walk through the court, a quick detective reveal, and a hard final image.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and see how evidence changed the cities.
